based_on: The owner's published text for each design, read from the database on 2026-10-16.
note: Suggested wording only: rewrites of the owner's own text in the awebound-brand voice (Sound like a person), aligned on October 16, 2026 to the King James Version the website now quotes (its terms and any quotation in KJV words). Bible links are offered in the website's translation too. The owner applies them in the content editor, one design at a time or all at once from the Content page; nothing is saved until the owner does. Server-only: never import into client code.

behold:thorns-to-lilies.biblicalContext:
Isaiah 1 is addressed to Judah and Jerusalem. The temple was busy. People brought their sacrifices, kept the feasts and made many prayers, while the poor were wronged and widows and the fatherless had no one to plead their cause. God tells them their offerings are a trouble to Him and He will not hear their prayers, because their hands are full of blood.

Then, in verse 18, He invites them to come and reason together with Him. Their sins are as scarlet and red like crimson, and He promises to make them white as snow and as wool. The God who has just named everything they’ve done wrong is the same God offering to wash it away.

The verses around it show what coming back looks like. He tells them to cease to do evil and learn to do well, to seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless and plead for the widow. The passage is honest about the other road too. Those who refuse and rebel will be devoured with the sword.
behold:thorns-to-lilies.designStory:
Thorns to Lilies puts the weight of sin and the hope of being made clean into one image. A crown of thorns circles the wordmark, and partway around, the thorns break open into lilies. The crown points to Christ’s suffering. The lilies stand for the new life that grows out of it.

The design comes from Isaiah 1:18, where God invites His people back to Him and promises to wash out a stain as deep as scarlet. Coming back starts with being honest about sin and receiving His forgiveness. It shows up afterward in everyday choices and in how other people are treated, and the lilies are a picture of a life God is still restoring.

behold:to-live-is-christ.biblicalContext:
Paul wrote Philippians from prison. He didn’t know whether he would be released or executed, and following Jesus had already cost him his freedom. What mattered most to him was that Christ would be magnified either way, whether by life or by death.

He weighs the two outcomes plainly. If he lives, his labor goes on, for the furtherance and joy of the believers in Philippi. If he dies, he will depart and be with Christ, which he calls far better. Being sure of that future doesn’t make him careless about the present. He expects to abide with them, because they still need him.

Later in the same letter, Paul looks back at everything he once counted gain and counts it loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus. He says he has suffered the loss of all things and counts them but dung, that he may win Christ.
behold:to-live-is-christ.designStory:
To Live Is Christ, To Die Is Gain sets an hourglass inside Paul’s words. Sand running through the glass makes time something you can see, and it raises a plain question about where the days are going.

Above the sand there’s a cross, and below it a seed has started to sprout. Paul’s sentence wraps around both. Ordinary days can be given to Christ while there’s time to give them, and the seed points to a life with Him that keeps going after the last grain falls.

behold:by-his-hem.biblicalContext:
Matthew 9 tells of a woman who had an issue of blood for twelve years. Mark’s account adds that she had suffered many things of many physicians and spent all that she had, and she was nothing bettered but grew worse. By the time she came near Jesus, she had nothing left to try.

She came behind Him in the crowd and touched the hem of His garment, saying within herself that if she might but touch it, she would be whole. Jesus turned, saw her and called her daughter. He told her that her faith had made her whole.

The crowd was thronging Him on every side, and Jesus still stopped for her. Mark records that He told her to go in peace and be whole of her plague.
behold:by-his-hem.designStory:
By His Hem keeps its focus on a hand and the hem of a garment. It’s a small gesture, and behind it are twelve years of need and the nerve to reach for Jesus with whatever strength was left.

A hand held out like that has nothing to offer and nothing to explain. It just reaches. The folds of the garment and the spray of rust pull the eye into the moment she touches it, where her suffering meets His compassion.

She came to Jesus as she was, need and all, and He turned to her.
behold:by-his-hem.imageryMeaning: The hand grasping the garment focuses on the moment of reaching. The folds and rust-colored accents give the encounter movement, while her words, printed in the King James wording, lead the viewer back to the passage.

behold:stone-in-motion.biblicalContext:
Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to see the sepulchre. There was a great earthquake, and an angel rolled back the stone from the door and sat on it. He told the women to fear not. Jesus wasn’t there. He had risen, as He said, and they could come and see the place where the Lord lay.

They departed quickly to tell the disciples, with fear and great joy, and on the way Jesus Himself met them. They held Him by the feet and worshiped Him. He told them to be not afraid and to tell His brethren to go into Galilee, where they would see Him.

Paul later writes in 1 Corinthians 15 that everything rests on this. If Christ be not raised, faith is vain. But now is Christ risen from the dead, the firstfruits of them that slept, and they that are His will be raised at His coming.
behold:stone-in-motion.designStory:
Stone in Motion starts at the tomb, a place that was supposed to be the end. The stone has rolled aside, and the sweep of blue around it keeps it moving, carrying the eye to the angel’s words at the center of the piece.

The moved stone is a witness to an empty grave. The blue gives the artwork its energy, and the words explain why the stone is moving at all.

It puts the news of the empty tomb on an everyday shirt. The One who was crucified is alive.
behold:stone-in-motion.imageryMeaning: The rolling stone and sweep of blue give the scene a sense of opening and movement. They direct attention toward the empty tomb and its announcement, printed in the same King James wording the website quotes.

behold:still-the-storm.biblicalContext:
In Mark 4, as evening comes, Jesus tells the disciples to pass over to the other side of the lake. They set out at His word. Partway across, a great storm of wind arises. The waves beat into the ship until it is full, while Jesus sleeps in the stern on a pillow. They wake Him and ask, “Master, carest thou not that we perish?”

He arises, rebukes the wind and says to the sea, “Peace, be still,” and there is a great calm. Then He asks why they are so fearful, and how it is that they have no faith. They fear exceedingly and ask one another what manner of man this is, that even the wind and the sea obey Him.

Psalm 107 describes sailors caught in a storm who cry unto the Lord in their trouble, and He makes the storm a calm. The disciples had just watched Jesus do what that psalm says God does.
behold:still-the-storm.designStory:
Still the Storm is built around the force of the water. On the front, storm waves break through the Awebound wordmark. On the back, a wave rises under the disciples’ question, the kind of sea no one in that boat could control.

Mark ends the story with their question still hanging in the air, and the design leaves it there too. “What manner of man is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”

The design comes from reverence for Christ, whose voice the storm obeyed. Fear and the need to stay in control can be brought to Him.
behold:still-the-storm.imageryMeaning: The breaking wave gives visible form to the danger and force of the storm. On the front, the same storm breaks through the Awebound wordmark. The back prints Mark 4:41 in the King James wording, the same words the website quotes.
behold:still-the-storm.shareCopy: The wind and the sea obey Him. Still the Storm points to Christ’s authority in Mark 4:41.

behold:torn-veil.biblicalContext:
Matthew records that when Jesus yielded up the ghost, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom. The earth did quake, the rocks rent, and the centurion watching Him said, “Truly this was the Son of God.” That veil closed off the holiest of all. Hebrews 9 explains that only the high priest went in behind it, once every year, and not without blood.

Hebrews 10 says believers now have boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way He consecrated for them through the veil, that is to say, His flesh. With Him as their high priest over the house of God, they’re told to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith.

The letter goes on to urge them to hold fast the profession of their faith without wavering and to provoke one another unto love and to good works.
behold:torn-veil.designStory:
Torn Veil shows the veil of the temple torn open, with light pouring through above the clouds. The tear gives the piece its movement. The light stands for the hope on the other side, the way to God that Christ opened.

Every fold and gap in the red fabric points to what His death made possible, and the opening reads as an invitation to come near.

The design holds reverence and gratitude together, because the way in cost Jesus His life. What it means carries on past the artwork, into prayer and worship and a life that answers His grace.
behold:torn-veil.imageryMeaning: The red veil opens around breaking light. Its direction of tearing echoes Matthew’s account, while the light is an artistic expression of the access and hope associated with Christ’s sacrifice.
behold:torn-veil.shareCopy: The veil is torn. Through Christ, believers are invited to draw near to God.

behold:the-passage.biblicalContext:
Psalm 23 pictures the Lord as a shepherd who provides for His sheep, makes them lie down in green pastures and leads them beside the still waters. He leads in the paths of righteousness and through the valley of the shadow of death, and the Shepherd’s care goes the whole way.

In the valley, David’s words change. Until then he has been talking about the Lord. Now he speaks to Him directly. “I will fear no evil: for thou art with me.” The rod and staff that guide and guard the sheep are what comfort him. Even the table God prepares for him is set in the presence of his enemies.

The psalm never pretends the valley isn’t there. It holds the danger inside a larger confidence in God’s care. Jesus later called Himself the good shepherd, who knows His sheep and gives His life for them.
behold:the-passage.designStory:
Fear Not carries David’s words from Psalm 23:4, “I will fear no evil,” in tall letters of cracked stone. Each letter holds a mountain valley with pines and a winding path, and red cracks run through the last word.

The name comes from those words. There’s a road to walk and a dark stretch to get through, and the Shepherd is near for all of it. God is with the one who walks.

The piece is a quiet confession of dependence on Him. When the way ahead isn’t clear, the words point back to His presence and the next faithful step.
behold:the-passage.imageryMeaning: The dark valley, the pines and the winding path inside the stone letters give the psalm a journey to follow. The red cracks run through “evil,” the word David says he won’t fear. The words keep God’s presence at the heart of the scene.
behold:the-passage.shareCopy: The Shepherd is present in the valley. Fear Not is inspired by Psalm 23:4.
behold:the-passage.publicPreview: A design about the Shepherd’s presence through the valley of the shadow of death.

behold:wonderfully-made.biblicalContext:
Psalm 139 is a prayer full of wonder at how completely God knows the one praying. He knows when David sits down and when he gets up, what he’s thinking from far away and what he’ll say before he says it. In verses 13 to 16, David turns to his own beginning. God formed him in his mother’s womb and saw him before he was born.

Being fearfully and wonderfully made sends David into praise. His attention stays on the Creator, who wrote down every one of his days before any of them happened. Genesis 1 says people are made in God’s image, and read together, the two passages give a reason to treat every human life with dignity and care.

The psalm ends with David asking God to search his heart, to see if there be any wicked way in him, and to lead him in the way everlasting.
behold:wonderfully-made.designStory:
Wonderfully Made wraps its lettering in roses and red leaves, so the words look tended, as if someone took their time with them. The flowers bring the beauty, and the Scripture turns it toward the Creator.

A wooden cross stands among the roses and ties the piece to Behold’s focus on Jesus. Between them, there’s room to stop and think about being formed and known by God.

That changes how a person sees themselves, and how they see everyone else. Gratitude for His work leads to gentleness and care toward the people around them.

behold:lambs-mark.biblicalContext:
In John 1, John the Baptist keeps pointing away from himself. He calls himself the voice of one crying in the wilderness, sent to make straight the way of the Lord. When he sees Jesus coming unto him, he says, “Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.” The people are asked to think about who Jesus is and what He came to do.

The title points to sacrifice. Isaiah 53 describes a servant brought as a lamb to the slaughter, who bare the sin of many. Christians see that costly work fulfilled in Christ.

John also bears record that he saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it abode upon Jesus, and he testifies that this is the Son of God.
behold:lambs-mark.designStory:
Lamb’s Mark brings a lamb and a crown of thorns together in one small emblem. The lamb comes from John calling Jesus the Lamb of God. The thorns tie that name to His suffering.

It’s a small image with a lot in it. The gentleness of the lamb sits right next to what the crown cost.

In Behold, this is the simplest way the release asks people to look at Jesus. The mark is easy to notice, and the hope is that it starts conversations that move from the stitching to His sacrifice and the forgiveness found in Him.

behold:signature-cap.biblicalContext:
Ephesians 1 opens with Paul blessing God for all the spiritual blessings His people have in Christ. In the middle of that praise, he says they have redemption through Jesus’ blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of God’s grace. Those gifts belong to a bigger story of being adopted as children, and of His plan to gather together in one all things in Christ, in heaven and on earth.

Redemption means being bought back at a cost. Paul grounds it in what Jesus did, and he turns the thanks toward the grace God gave freely.

Ephesians 2 shows what that grace produces. Salvation is by grace through faith, the gift of God, and those He makes alive in Christ are His workmanship, created unto good works, which God before ordained.
behold:signature-cap.designStory:
The Signature Cap is Awebound’s name in its own lettering, with red thorns reaching out from both sides. Crimson runs through the ivory letters, so the meaning of the thorns carries right into the name.

The thorns recall the crown Christ wore. The red is for the blood He shed to redeem us, and it keeps the name rooted in His sacrifice.

The tagline says why the cap exists. Bound in awe is reverence for Jesus. Worn without shame is being willing to be known as His. The cap goes wherever the person wearing it goes, as a reminder to reflect Him in how they speak and how they treat people.
behold:signature-cap.imageryMeaning: The red thorn branches recall the crown Christ wore, and the crimson running through the ivory letters is a reminder of His sacrifice. They tie Awebound’s name to what Behold is about, looking to Jesus and the redemption found in Him.
